pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends heat treatment to low-dimensional HEA films/nanoribbons using a rapid, localized laser annealing process tailored to nanoscale systems, addressing challenges of the film’s large surface-to-volume ratio and heat-transfer limitations.

fields.hypothesis: Post-deposition rapid, localized annealing of the nanoscale films using a controlled laser pulse will reduce surface defect density and aid magnetic exchange homogeneity, leading to a more ideal second-order magnetocaloric response with reduced hysteresis under low-applied fields.
fields.material_initial_state: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films or nanoribbons with high density of surface and edge defects and inhomogeneous exchange interactions.
fields.intervention: Subject the as-deposited low-dimensional HEA films/nanoribbons to rapid, localized laser annealing (at a temperature sufficiently high for defect relaxation but below the melting point) for a fixed short duration.
fields.conditions: Laser pulse parameters (wavelength, power, duration) chosen to enable submicron-scale heat treatment; experiments conducted at low applied magnetic fields (< 1 T) during controlled cycling at temperatures around the expected critical region; heat-transfer constraints are explicitly monitored by varying pulse repetition rate.
fields.structural_mediator: Reduction in surface/edge defect density and local strain variations; improvement in magnetic homogeneity (narrower distribution of exchange energies) at the film surfaces.
fields.mechanism: Following the mechanism reported in the paper where annealing reduced the distribution of exchange parameters (as seen by XRD peak sharpening and universal scaling collapse), the laser-annealing in thin films is expected to relieve local stresses and eliminate processing-induced defects. This should lead to a sharper second-order magnetic transition, reduced hysteresis under low fields, and enhanced refrigerant capacity due to better localized heat exchange.
fields.predicted_outcome: A measured magnetocaloric entropy change (ΔS) peak that is sharper and occurs at a more well-defined temperature, and a reduction in hysteresis losses during cyclic magnetization. Compared to as-deposited films, the laser-annealed films should exhibit a decrease in the F-statistic variability (from universal scaling analysis) by roughly 30–50% in the same temperature interval.
fields.baseline: As-deposited thin films with broad ΔS(T) curves and higher hysteresis due to defect-induced magnetic inhomogeneity.
fields.boundary: The intervention should be applied at temperatures where the films are below any phase transformation threshold (avoiding partial melting or grain coarsening) and for film thicknesses in the nanoscale regime (<100 nm) where surface effects dominate.
fields.uncertainty: The exact quantification of improvement (percentage reduction in hysteresis and enhancement in ΔS peak) may be material- and process-dependent; heat-transfer limitations might still play a role at very high cycle frequencies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoscale HEA films: one set undergoes the laser annealing treatment and the other remains as-deposited. Measure M(H) and M(T) under identical low-field magnetic-cooling cycles. Conduct high-resolution XRD and universal scaling statistical analysis to compare exchange homogeneity.
measurements: Shape and peak width of ΔS(T) curves
Hysteresis loop area in M(H) cycles
XRD FWHM and peak profiles
BF analysis F-statistic of scaled ΔS curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-annealed films do not exhibit a statistically significant narrowing of the ΔS peak and reduction of hysteresis (or if the F-statistic does not decrease relative to the as-deposited films), then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observations regarding how structural defects and heat treatment affect the magnetic homogeneity and magnetocaloric response, combined with background principles of heat transfer in nanoscale systems.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a processing route via lithographic patterning design to control not only composition and post-deposition annealing but also the geometry-induced thermal and mechanical stresses in low-dimensional HEA systems—a strategy not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Engineering the lateral dimensions of lithographically patterned nanoribbons to include variable width (and hence a modulated edge-to-volume ratio) will actively control local heat dissipation and stress profiles during low-field magnetocaloric cycling, thereby reducing hysteresis and stabilizing the magnetocaloric entropy change.
fields.material_initial_state: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi nanoribbons with standard uniform widths that exhibit suboptimal heat-transfer due to high edge-to-volume ratios and consequent stress-induced exchange inhomogeneities.
fields.intervention: Design lithographic patterns to fabricate nanoribbons with a tailored width gradient along their length (or with periodic wide and narrow sections) to promote enhanced lateral heat dissipation and reduce localized thermal gradients.
fields.conditions: Nanoribbons of the HEA material produced on substrates with controlled thermal conductivity; tests carried out under low-applied magnetic fields (<1 T) and slow cycling rates (to allow for observed heat-transfer effects) in a temperature range near the magnetocaloric transition.
fields.structural_mediator: Spatial variation in ribbon width alters the edge-to-volume ratio, which influences local strain and thermal dissipation. This reduces non-uniform stress and defect formation, thereby promoting a more homogeneous magnetic state and consistent exchange interactions across the sample.
fields.mechanism: Based on the principle that materials with enhanced heat-transfer (as noted in the background for melt spinning and in discussions of thermal conduction) can avoid localized overheating and defect-related inhomogeneities, patterned ribbons with modulated widths are predicted to dissipate heat more uniformly. This structural design minimizes local variations in magnetic and thermal properties that contribute to hysteresis and broad ΔS distributions during cyclic cooling.
fields.predicted_outcome: Nanoribbons with engineered width gradients are expected to show a reduction in hysteresis losses (smaller M(H) loop area) and a narrower ΔS(T) peak with improved refrigerant capacity compared to uniform-width ribbons. The operating window for efficient magnetocaloric cycling should widen slightly, though the magnitude of ΔS may be similar.
fields.baseline: Uniform-width as-deposited nanoribbons exhibiting significant hysteresis and broader, less predictable ΔS behavior due to edge-related thermal and structural inhomogeneities.
fields.boundary: The effect is expected to be beneficial for ribbon widths in the 50–200 nm range, where edge effects and heat-transfer limitations are appreciable; beyond these dimensions, the benefits may diminish.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in hysteresis reduction and ΔS narrowing are not precisely predictable without detailed thermal modeling; potential fabrication limits could also impose variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of nanoribbons: one with a uniform width and one with a designed width gradient. Subject both designs to identical low-field magnetic-cooling cycles, while simultaneously using infrared thermography and microstructural imaging (e.g., TEM) to track local temperature profiles and defect densities.

Shape and width of ΔS(T) curves
Thermal imaging profiles during operation
Defect density mapping via TEM or similar
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the patterned nanoribbons with width gradients do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in hysteresis and achieve a notably narrower ΔS(T) peak (or if no modification in local thermal profiles is observed) compared to uniform ribbons, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C12
pool.builds_on: the principle that exchange coupling of soft and hard magnetic phases can optimize magnetic reversal (as seen in the discussion of coupled phases in PMC7408491), extended here through compositional modulation in a high-entropy alloy.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes deliberate in-situ compositional tailoring (Ni-enrichment) to create nanoscale exchange-coupled regions, a strategy not explored in the reported work, to specifically address magnetocaloric hysteresis and performance in thin-film geometries.

fields.hypothesis: Localized compositional tuning via in-situ Ni enrichment within the non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloy forms exchange-coupled nanocomposite regions that balance soft and hard magnetic behavior to minimize hysteresis during low-applied-field cycling while maintaining a strong magnetocaloric response.
fields.material_initial_state: As-deposited, nanostructured thin films or patterned nanoribbons of FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys with a homogeneous non-equiatomic composition, exhibiting magnetocaloric properties similar to bulk but without the benefit of engineered phase separation.
fields.intervention: Implement a deposition process (e.g., via pulsed laser deposition with compositional modulation or in-situ co-sputtering with spatially varying targets) to create micro-scale regions with slightly higher Ni content, thereby intentionally forming an exchange-coupled composite of soft (Ni-rich) and hard (remaining matrix) magnetic phases.
fields.conditions: The compositional modulation must yield a periodic or random exchange-coupled network within the nanoribbon geometry; experiments should be performed under low applied magnetic fields (<100 mT) with cycling frequencies sensitive to heat-transfer limitations.
fields.structural_mediator: Exchange-coupled nanocomposite microstructure with distinct soft (Ni-enriched) and hard magnetic regions providing a dual magnetic response.
fields.mechanism: Increasing Ni locally reduces the magnetic anisotropy and coercivity in the enriched regions (as Ni typically has lower anisotropy), leading to an interplay with the harder matrix regions. The exchange coupling between these domains can smooth the magnetization reversal process, thereby diminishing hysteresis losses. Simultaneously, the composite nature creates a more gradual magnetocaloric response with improved efficiency under low-field cycling. This mechanism extends principles of exchange-spring magnets to nanoscale high-entropy systems (PMC7408491::web::007::2_experimental and related discussions on exchange coupling).
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to uniformly composed films, the exchange-coupled composite should exhibit a narrower hysteresis loop (lower energy loss) and a magnetocaloric temperature change that is more reversibly traversed during low-field cycles. Coercivity is predicted to decrease in the soft regions while maintaining overall high magnetization.
fields.baseline: Uniform as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films or nanoribbons with homogenous composition and typical hysteresis behavior observed in bulk forms.
fields.boundary: Effective if the local compositional gradients do not lead to phase segregation that might disrupt exchange coupling; applicable in regimes where the scaling of soft/hard region dimensions is within the exchange length of the material.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal degree of Ni enrichment and the length scale of compositional modulation are not precisely known and require systematic optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with engineered local Ni enrichment (compositional modulation) and one with uniform composition. Measure the magnetic hysteresis loops and magnetocaloric effect under identical low-applied-field cycling conditions, and assess the microstructure using spatially resolved techniques (e.g., TEM-EDX mapping).
measurements: Hysteresis loop shape and coercivity via magnetometry
Magnetocaloric temperature change using calorimetry
Microstructural mapping of compositional variations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered samples do not show a reduction in hysteresis (narrower loop or lower coercivity) and no improvement in the reversibility of the magnetocaloric response compared to the uniformly composed control, then the hypothesis should be rejected.

pool.label: C13
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that magnetic free energy drives spinodal decomposition in systems with nearly identical atomic sizes, extended here by chemically engineering the alloy to mimic that near-equal regime.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes a compositional engineering route—minor Ga substitution—to intentionally balance atomic radii in a non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA, thereby promoting the desired nanostructuring for optimized magnetocaloric performance, a strategy not addressed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Minor Elemental Substitution to Minimize Atomic Size Mismatch and Enhance Magnetic Free‐Energy–Driven Nanostructuring
fields.material_initial_state: As‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloy thin films or nanoribbons containing Fe, Mn, Ni, Ge, and Si, where significant atomic size differences (especially involving metalloids Ge and Si) hinder the favorable nanodomain formation driven by magnetic free energy.
fields.intervention: Alter the alloy composition by partially substituting a fraction of Ge (or Si) with an element like Ga, which has an atomic radius very close to that of the 3d transition elements (near 1.24–1.25 Å) to reduce local lattice strain.
fields.conditions: Prepare two variants of the alloy: the original FeMnNiGeSi composition and a modified composition FeMnNiGe₁₋ₓGaₓSi (with x ≈ 0.1–0.2) to moderately adjust the atomic size landscape. Deposition parameters (e.g., sputter deposition) must be kept identical, and subsequent magnetic-cooling tests conducted under low-applied-field (<100 Oe) conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: By introducing Ga, the overall atomic-size disparity within the film is reduced, thereby lowering the lattice distortion energy. This adjustment creates a local environment more akin to the near-equal atomic radii scenario, which facilitates the magnetic free-energy–driven spinodal-like decomposition into FM-rich nanodomains.
fields.mechanism: In the original FeMnNiGeSi system, the large size differences impede coherent magnetic domain formation. Adding a small fraction of Ga (whose atomic radius aligns with Fe, Mn, and Ni) offsets the metalloid mismatch and reduces local strain energy. This enables the magnetic free-energy contribution (as discussed in PMC13030938::web::010) to more effectively drive a favorable nanostructure with better exchange coupling, resulting in lower coercivity and improved magnetocaloric effects.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline composition, the Ga-substituted alloy is predicted to exhibit a more coherent nanodomain structure with a narrower distribution of FM cluster sizes, reduced coercivity, and an enhanced reversible magnetocaloric temperature change (ΔT) in low-field cycles.
fields.baseline: As‐deposited FeMnNiGeSi films/nanoribbons without Ga substitution, which show irregular nanostructure and relatively higher hysteresis due to the pronounced metalloid-induced lattice mismatch.
fields.boundary: The substitution level must be moderate (e.g., 10–20 atomic %) to effectively reduce atomic size mismatch without drastically altering the overall phase stability or composition-dependent magnetic interactions.
fields.uncertainty: The precise level of Ga substitution that optimally minimizes mismatch while retaining desired magnetic properties may vary; quantitative computational studies or phase diagram assessments are needed to fine-tune the composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of films: one with the original FeMnNiGeSi composition and one with the modified composition FeMnNiGe₀.9Ga₀.1Si (or within the 10–20% substitution range). Use XRD and TEM to evaluate any change in lattice parameters and nanodomain uniformity, and perform low-field magnetic-cooling cycle tests to compare hysteresis loops and ΔT responses.
measurements: XRD for lattice parameter analysis and strain assessment
TEM for nanodomain morphology and size distribution
Magnetic hysteresis measurements (coercivity, remanence)
Direct ΔT measurements during low-applied-field cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ga-substituted samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in lattice strain, refinement of the nanodomain structure, and improved magnetic softness (lower hysteresis and higher reversible ΔT) compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C7
top3.builds_on: the principles of rapid heat extraction used in melt spinning (TXT::doitpoms::casting/casting_other::000) and the general relation between thermal uniformity and magnetic switching dynamics as per materials science fundamentals (TXT::mit_ocw::3-012-fundamentals-of-materials-science-fall-2005/lec03t.pdf::003).
top3.what_is_new: This proposal introduces a microfabricated suspended membrane architecture to directly address dynamic heat-transfer limitations in thin-film HEA systems, a strategy not investigated in prior Heusler film studies, thereby linking improved thermal management to enhanced magnetocaloric performance in a low-dimensional context.

fields.hypothesis: Enhancing dynamic heat extraction by integrating the as‐deposited FeMnNiGeSi HEA films onto microfabricated suspended high-thermal-conductivity membranes will reduce thermal gradients during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles, leading to a decrease in hysteresis of the magnetocaloric response.
fields.material_initial_state: As‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA films on standard substrates exhibiting a disordered microstructure with potentially non-uniform temperature profiles during dynamic magnetic-cooling cycles.
fields.intervention: Transfer or directly deposit the HEA films onto microfabricated suspended membranes made of materials with high thermal conductivity (e.g., diamond-like carbon or boron nitride coated silicon nitride) designed to improve lateral heat spreading and extraction.
fields.conditions: The films remain nanoscale (<200 nm thick) and the membranes are engineered to minimize thermal boundary resistance. Experiments are carried out under applied magnetic fields below 50 mT and at cycling frequencies ranging from quasi-static to moderately dynamic conditions. Prior thermal modeling is used to ensure that the heat extraction capacity of the membranes exceeds that of conventional substrates.
fields.structural_mediator: An integrated interfacial architecture that dramatically reduces local temperature gradients across the HEA film during rapid magnetic-cooling cycles, promoting uniform thermal conditions and minimal local overheating.
fields.mechanism: In low-dimensional HEA films, limited heat extraction can lead to transient thermal gradients during cycling, which may cause non-uniform magnetization reversal and enhanced hysteresis. By employing suspended, high-thermal-conductivity membranes, the local thermal resistance is reduced, resulting in faster heat removal. This improved thermal uniformity reduces temperature-induced variations in magnetic properties and facilitates more reversible domain switching, thereby reducing hysteresis in the magnetocaloric response.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to films on conventional substrates, the membrane-supported films should exhibit lower hysteresis (e.g., lower coercive fields and reduced hysteresis loop area) during dynamic low-field cycles. The magnetocaloric entropy change is predicted to be more reproducible across cycles, especially at higher frequencies. The magnitude of improvements is qualitatively supported by enhanced thermal management, though the exact quantitative reduction in hysteresis will depend on the membrane's thermal conductance.
fields.baseline: HEA films on standard bulk substrates which experience higher interfacial thermal resistance and more pronounced thermal gradients during cycling, leading to larger hysteresis and less reversible magnetocaloric effects.
fields.boundary: The approach is effective only if the membrane thermal conductance significantly outperforms conventional substrates and the film transfer process does not alter the intrinsic magnetic microstructure. Additionally, mechanical stability of the membranes under cyclic thermal load must be maintained.
fields.uncertainty: While thermal management is known to affect performance in dynamic magnetic systems, the precise influence of reduced thermal gradients on magnetocaloric hysteresis in these specific HEA films remains to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of FeMnNiGeSi HEA films on conventional substrates and one set on the suspended high-thermal-conductivity membranes. Use infrared thermal imaging or micro-Raman thermometry to map temperature distribution during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles. Subsequently, conduct magnetometry (SQUID or VSM) to compare hysteresis parameters and perform magnetocaloric cycling tests at various frequencies.
measurements: Temperature profiles and cooling rates during magnetic-cooling cycles
Hysteresis loop parameters (coercivity, loop area) from magnetometry
Magnetocaloric entropy change and reversibility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the membrane-supported films do not exhibit statistically significant improvement in thermal uniformity (as measured by temperature mapping) and corresponding reductions in hysteresis and enhanced reversibility of the magnetocaloric response compared to the control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C11
top3.builds_on: The paper’s observations regarding how structural defects and heat treatment affect the magnetic homogeneity and magnetocaloric response, combined with background principles of heat transfer in nanoscale systems.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a processing route via lithographic patterning design to control not only composition and post-deposition annealing but also the geometry-induced thermal and mechanical stresses in low-dimensional HEA systems—a strategy not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Engineering the lateral dimensions of lithographically patterned nanoribbons to include variable width (and hence a modulated edge-to-volume ratio) will actively control local heat dissipation and stress profiles during low-field magnetocaloric cycling, thereby reducing hysteresis and stabilizing the magnetocaloric entropy change.
fields.material_initial_state: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi nanoribbons with standard uniform widths that exhibit suboptimal heat-transfer due to high edge-to-volume ratios and consequent stress-induced exchange inhomogeneities.
fields.intervention: Design lithographic patterns to fabricate nanoribbons with a tailored width gradient along their length (or with periodic wide and narrow sections) to promote enhanced lateral heat dissipation and reduce localized thermal gradients.
fields.conditions: Nanoribbons of the HEA material produced on substrates with controlled thermal conductivity; tests carried out under low-applied magnetic fields (<1 T) and slow cycling rates (to allow for observed heat-transfer effects) in a temperature range near the magnetocaloric transition.
fields.structural_mediator: Spatial variation in ribbon width alters the edge-to-volume ratio, which influences local strain and thermal dissipation. This reduces non-uniform stress and defect formation, thereby promoting a more homogeneous magnetic state and consistent exchange interactions across the sample.
fields.mechanism: Based on the principle that materials with enhanced heat-transfer (as noted in the background for melt spinning and in discussions of thermal conduction) can avoid localized overheating and defect-related inhomogeneities, patterned ribbons with modulated widths are predicted to dissipate heat more uniformly. This structural design minimizes local variations in magnetic and thermal properties that contribute to hysteresis and broad ΔS distributions during cyclic cooling.
fields.predicted_outcome: Nanoribbons with engineered width gradients are expected to show a reduction in hysteresis losses (smaller M(H) loop area) and a narrower ΔS(T) peak with improved refrigerant capacity compared to uniform-width ribbons. The operating window for efficient magnetocaloric cycling should widen slightly, though the magnitude of ΔS may be similar.
fields.baseline: Uniform-width as-deposited nanoribbons exhibiting significant hysteresis and broader, less predictable ΔS behavior due to edge-related thermal and structural inhomogeneities.
fields.boundary: The effect is expected to be beneficial for ribbon widths in the 50–200 nm range, where edge effects and heat-transfer limitations are appreciable; beyond these dimensions, the benefits may diminish.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in hysteresis reduction and ΔS narrowing are not precisely predictable without detailed thermal modeling; potential fabrication limits could also impose variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of nanoribbons: one with a uniform width and one with a designed width gradient. Subject both designs to identical low-field magnetic-cooling cycles, while simultaneously using infrared thermography and microstructural imaging (e.g., TEM) to track local temperature profiles and defect densities.
measurements: Hysteresis loop area under cyclic magnetic fields
Shape and width of ΔS(T) curves
Thermal imaging profiles during operation
Defect density mapping via TEM or similar
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the patterned nanoribbons with width gradients do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in hysteresis and achieve a notably narrower ΔS(T) peak (or if no modification in local thermal profiles is observed) compared to uniform ribbons, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C9
top3.builds_on: The paper demonstrates that pulse electrodeposition yields a uniform, nanocrystalline dual-phase structure (PMC8065170::web::012). This hypothesis builds on that by integrating lithographic patterning—guided by intrinsic crystallographic orientation—to tailor shape anisotropy and heat dissipation, specifically addressing the low-dimensional challenges in magnetocaloric cooling.
top3.what_is_new: It introduces a combined approach of crystallography-guided lithographic patterning to align nanoribbon geometries with the film's magnetic easy axes, thereby simultaneously targeting reductions in hysteresis and optimizations in thermal dissipation in FeMnNiGeSi HEA nanostructures—a strategy not proposed in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Aligning lithographically patterned nanoribbons along the in-plane crystallographic easy axes of as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi HEA thin films will optimize shape anisotropy in harmony with the intrinsic nanocrystalline magnetic structure, thereby reducing hysteresis and improving the magnetocaloric response during low-field magnetic cycles by facilitating efficient thermal dissipation.
fields.material_initial_state: Continuous, as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA thin films with a nanocrystalline dual-phase structure produced via pulse electrodeposition.
fields.intervention: Employ advanced lithographic patterning (guided by pre-patterning crystallographic orientation mapping, for example, via XRD) to fabricate nanoribbons whose long axes are aligned with the film's magnetic easy axis. The pattern will include optimized ribbon widths (e.g., 100–500 nm) while retaining the film’s original thickness.
fields.conditions: All deposition conditions and overall alloy composition are maintained; patterning is performed post-deposition without altering the intrinsic microstructure. The design is applicable for nanoscale films and relies on accurately identifying the in-plane easy axis.
fields.structural_mediator: The patterned geometry imposes a designed shape anisotropy that cooperates with the intrinsic nanocrystalline structure, and the increased edge-to-volume ratio enhances heat exchange with the environment.
fields.mechanism: The alignment of nanoribbons with the magnetic easy axis reduces random domain wall pinning since the geometrical shape anisotropy supports coherent magnetic switching. Furthermore, the enhanced surface area from the patterned edges facilitates more rapid heat dissipation during fast magnetic cycles, thereby reducing thermal lag that can otherwise broaden the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to continuous films, the aligned nanoribbons should show reduced coercivity (narrower hysteresis loops) and a magnetocaloric response with a sharper and possibly slightly shifted temperature peak under low applied field oscillations. The improvements are expected qualitatively, though quantitative gains will depend on precise pattern geometry.
fields.baseline: Continuous, unpatterned FeMnNiGeSi HEA thin films with isotropic magnetic switching behavior and standard hysteresis and magnetocaloric performance.
fields.boundary: Success depends on maintaining the nanocrystalline structure during patterning. Excessively narrow or damaged ribbons may introduce extra defects that could counteract the benefits. The process is viable as long as lithographic resolution allows for accurate alignment relative to crystallographic orientation.
fields.uncertainty: The exact notch geometry, ribbon dimensions, and alignment tolerance required to achieve significant improvements in magnetic and thermal performance are uncertain and must be optimized experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: First, map the in-plane crystallographic orientation of as-deposited films (using XRD). Then, using lithography, pattern nanoribbons aligned along the identified easy axes and also create a control set of ribbons with random orientations. Characterize magnetic hysteresis (using VSM) and measure the magnetocaloric response under low-field cycling. Compare performance across oriented and non-oriented patterns.
measurements: Crystallographic orientation mapping (XRD)
Ribbon geometry and edge quality (SEM/TEM)
Magnetic hysteresis loops (VSM)
Magnetocaloric temperature change (calorimetric or cyclic magnetic tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoribbons aligned along the easy axis do not show a statistically significant reduction in coercivity and an improved or sharper magnetocaloric response compared to both continuous films and randomly oriented patterns, then the hypothesis is falsified.
